source.title: Neighborhood Region Smoothing Regularization for Finding Flat Minima In Deep Neural Networks

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a training regularizer changes held-out image-classification accuracy and whether a curvature measurement changes with the training strategy, using methods distinct from the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper compares standard training, random perturbation training (RPR), and NRS on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, and reports a Hessian eigenvalue comparison. These results do not directly test any listed version. Hyperparameter sweeps in Figure 1 are not separately extracted because the figure reports curves without tabulated values.
record.test_reason: The study uses the premise that flatter minima improve generalization to develop NRS and evaluates its own training method. None of its comparisons tests V1–V8. In particular, last-layer Hessian eigenvalues and test accuracies do not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness relationship with train–test gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that NRS improves generalization across the tested architectures and datasets, and interpret its smaller last-layer Hessian eigenvalue as evidence of flatter minima. This interpretation does not establish V7.
record.recipe_differences: Adds a neighborhood model divergence penalty and neighborhood empirical loss to standard empirical-loss training; compares this NRS strategy with standard training and RPR.
record.method_sensitivity: CIFAR test accuracy varies across datasets, augmentation strategies, model architectures, and NRS hyperparameters ϵ and α; the paper reports that improvement is generally larger on Cifar100 than Cifar10. Figure 1 gives accuracy curves for selected ϵ and α settings without tabulated values.

fits_no_version.finding: NRS improves reported test accuracy in every Table 1 and Table 2 comparison; RPR remains near baseline in Table 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NRS can improve image-classification test accuracy under the tested training and selection procedures; random perturbation training alone provides no reported improvement.

fits_no_version.finding: The reported last-layer largest Hessian eigenvalue is 2.42 for NRS, versus 49.15 for baseline and 51.79 for RPR, on WideResNet-28-10/CIFAR-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: NRS produces lower measured last-layer Hessian curvature in this selected model comparison.

record.problems: The paper reports best results selected by grid search for CIFAR and does not report corresponding training accuracy or train-test gaps in the result tables. The Hessian result is from one architecture and dataset, measures only the last layer, and has no uncertainty estimate. RPR near-baseline differences are described by the authors as having no effect on improving generalization.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows left out; Figure 1 hyperparameter accuracy curves are not extracted as individual numerical rows because values are presented only as plots.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the paired natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy comparison.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of learned or imposed local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under comparable tuning. Different optimizers across different architectures do not isolate this effect.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that recover performance. Batch size is searched or fixed, without reported batch-size comparisons.
Adding or removing dropout, small-data effects, excessive dropout, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with train–test gaps at similarly low training loss, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing examples selected by label memorization and comparing retraining with random removal.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted numerical values match the supplied tables. States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions because every row links to none; this does not deny the reported NRS accuracy improvements or near-baseline RPR results. Tables 1–2 are method-performance comparisons and should not serve as claim-test rows. CIFAR results are selected through hyperparameter search; training accuracies and train–test gaps are not reported. Normalizing perturbations during NRS training does not turn the separate Hessian evaluation into a magnitude-aware sharpness measurement.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on random labels or compare random-label and natural-label generalization.
Does not sweep network width around the interpolation threshold.
Does not compare convolutional networks with fully connected networks.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out performance.
Does not compare batch sizes or test a large-batch generalization gap.
Does not compare adding or removing dropout; it only notes dropout as present in VGG16.
Reports the largest Hessian eigenvalue for one model and dataset, but does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or correlate it with train-test gaps across matched-training-loss networks.
Does not remove memorized training examples.
